planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; SL28 coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Selected in the 1930s by Scott Agricultural Laboratories in Kenya from a single drought-tolerant tree, this tall, vigorous Arabica selection is renowned among specialty roasters for an intensely bright, blackcurrant-like acidity and full, syrupy body that few other varieties match. It is deep-rooted and notably tolerant of dry spells once established, but it lacks resistance to coffee berry disease and leaf rust, so watch new growth for spotting and treat promptly if either appears. Grow it in the same warm, humid, filtered-shade conditions favored by other highland Arabicas, feeding regularly through the growing season, and expect a tall, open-branched shrub that begins bearing after three to four years. Because of its height it suits large containers, conservatories, or in-ground planting in zones 10-11 rather than tight patio pots.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; SL34 coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Selected alongside its sister cultivar SL28 by Scott Agricultural Laboratories in Kenya, SL34 shares much of the same French Mission Bourbon ancestry and produces a similarly rich, wine-toned, high-quality cup, though it tends to perform better in wetter highland sites and bears somewhat more heavily. Like SL28 it is a tall, open-growing Arabica with limited resistance to leaf rust and coffee berry disease, so it rewards attentive scouting and prompt treatment of any fungal spotting on leaves or cherries. Provide the same warm, humid, dappled-shade conditions as other highland Arabica types, feed regularly, and expect first cherries after roughly three to four years. Its larger eventual size makes it best suited to spacious containers or in-ground planting in zones 10-11.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Pacas coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Discovered in 1949 as a naturally occurring dwarf mutation of Bourbon on the Pacas family farm in El Salvador, this compact, densely branched Arabica selection bears heavily for its small stature and is now one of the most widely planted varieties in Central America. Its short habit allows closer spacing than tall heirloom Arabicas and suits container culture well, though heavy bearing on a small frame means it needs regular feeding to sustain both plant vigor and cup quality. Pacas is also the dwarf parent of the large-beaned Pacamara hybrid, passing on its manageable size to that cross. Grow it in the same warm, humid, filtered-shade conditions as other Arabica coffees and expect the first cherries after three to four years.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full sun; CCN-51 cacao is a frost-tender tropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Bred in Ecuador in the 1960s by cacao researcher Homero Castro and named for the Colección Castro Naranjal breeding program, CCN-51 was developed for high yield and strong resistance to witches-broom and monilia pod rot, problems that devastated many older Ecuadorian cacao plantings. Unlike shade-loving heirloom types such as Criollo, it tolerates considerably more direct sun and bears earlier and more heavily, which has made it popular with commercial growers even though its beans need careful, extended fermentation to develop good chocolate flavor and avoid the acidic, astringent notes it is sometimes criticized for. Give it rich, moist, well-drained soil, consistent warmth and humidity, and protection from wind while young. Expect a vigorous, relatively fast-bearing tree that reaches production in as little as three years under good conditions.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Benifuuki tea carries Assam parentage and is less cold-hardy than typical small-leaved Japanese tea cultivars.

directions: Released by Japan's national tea research program and bred in part from Assam-type stock, Benifuuki was originally developed for black tea production but is now grown mainly for green tea and matcha because its leaves are unusually rich in methylated catechins, compounds studied for their anti-allergy properties. Its Assam ancestry gives it larger leaves and faster growth than classic small-leaved Japanese cultivars like Yabukita, but also leaves it noticeably less cold-hardy, so plants need reliable winter protection outside the warmest zones. Grow in acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade with consistent moisture, and mulch well to keep roots cool. Begin light plucking of the top two leaves and a bud once bushes are three to four years old and well established.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service Tea Research
